title: Declarative rollout manifests & deterministic rollback protocol - meeting notes
content:
Meeting: Platform Architecture review - Declarative rollouts + deterministic rollback
Date: 2024-11-15 10:00am PST
Attendees: Aisha (notes), Marco, Eleanor, Devon, Priya, Sam W. (SRE), Lina (Product)
Context / why we met:
- We need a single, developer-friendly way to declare model rollout behavior that works across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Current ad-hoc canary scripts and ad-hoc operator jobs lead to inconsistent state and hard-to-reproduce failures.
- Goal: agree on a manifest shape + controller responsibilities + a deterministic rollback protocol that can be audited and replayed.

Agenda:
- Review proposed manifest schema from RFC
- Define controller invariants (safety checks, idempotency, observability hooks)
- Discuss rollback triggers & deterministic reversal steps
- Operational playbooks and SLO/alert integration

Summary decisions (TL;DR):
1) Adopt a declarative rollout manifest (YAML) that expresses: target model variant(s), percentage schedule, validation hooks (prometheus/metric thresholds or synthetic prompt sets), max-failure windows, and safety fences (per-tenant and global).
2) Controller will implement a 3-phase transition semantics: PREPARE -> GRADUAL -> STABILIZE. Each phase has well-defined checkpoints and rollback points.
3) Rollback will be deterministic: controller records an ordered changelog (immutable) and rollback replays the inverse operations up to the last known-stable checkpoint.
4) All rollout state is stored in the control plane DB with cryptographic signing of change records for Private deployments (customer-managed KMS optional).

Notes and rationale (detailed):
- Manifest shape: we iterated on the RFC example and landed on a minimal set of required fields and optional verification hooks. Fields:
  - kind: RolloutManifest v1
  - metadata: name, tenant_id, created_by, created_at
  - spec:
    - target_variants: list of {name, model_ref, resources_hint}
    - strategy: {type: linear | canary | blue-green, duration_minutes}
    - schedule: ordered list of {pct, min_duration_minutes, validation_check}
    - validations: list of checks (metric-based or synthetic prompts) with pass/fail thresholds
    - safety_fences: {global_disable: bool, allowed_regions: list, max_concurrent_rollouts_per_team: int}
    - observability_hooks: endpoints for trace/span injection and synthetic-eval bucket
  - status: controlled by controller (phase, current_pct, last_checkpoint_id, health)

- Why synthetic prompt checks + metrics? Metric thresholds (latency, error-rate, quality regression from eval harness) are necessary but brittle alone. We require at least one synthetic prompt validation per schedule step for model-quality safety. This is optional for low-risk variants (e.g., config-only changes) but encouraged.

Controller invariants and guarantees:
- Idempotency: applying the same manifest multiple times must converge to same status; manifests can be reapplied as part of reconciliation loop.
- Single-writer per rollout name/tenant: concurrency control via optimistic locking and per-tenant leader election to avoid split-brain in Dedicated clusters.
- Checkpointing: after each schedule step completes its validation, the controller writes an immutable checkpoint record with checkpoint_id, signature, timestamp, and digest of the state. Checkpoints form the deterministic rollback anchors.
- Visibility: all checkpoints and events are emitted to the Console and to a dedicated rollout index in telemetry.

Rollback protocol (deterministic):
- Trigger sources: manual (Console/API), automatic via failed validation, or operator (SRE).
- Deterministic rollback algorithm:
  1) Identify last checkpoint marked STABLE in the changelog for that rollout.
  2) Compute inverse steps by traversing changelog entries in reverse order until target checkpoint. Each changelog entry is typed (e.g., route-split-update, cache-prime, kv-warm).
  3) Apply inverse operations in reverse order, respecting preconditions; controller uses dry-run and validation hook for each inverse op where possible.
  4) After rollback completes, write a rollback-record with cause, operator, and link to logs.
- Reasoning: this makes rollback predictable and reproducible — critical for Private/on-prem where operator access is constrained.

Operational safety fences and constraints:
- Global kill-switch: platform can flip a global boolean that forces abort of ongoing rollouts and initiates safe rollback to last-stable checkpoint across affected tenants. Requires two-person approval in prod.
- Rate limits: Enforce per-team concurrent rollouts and global per-region concurrency. Configuration surfaced in Console.
- Resource prechecks: controller will simulate resource fit (GPU memory, model slice placements) before entering GRADUAL phase, and fail-fast if limits would be breached.

Observability & SLO integration:
- Each schedule step emits structured events: step.start, step.validation.pass/fail, step.complete, checkpoint.create
- Integrate with existing tracing: add rollout_id and checkpoint_id across request traces to surface in tail-latency dashboards.
- SLOs to add: rollout-mean-time-to-stable, rollback-time, synthetic-eval-failure-rate. Alerts: synthetic-eval-failure-rate > X% triggers auto-rollback policy (configurable per-tenant).

Security / signing (Private deployments):
- Add optional record signing for immutable checkpoints and changelogs: support customer KMS/HSM for key material. This helps auditing and tamper-evidence in air-gapped environments.
- RBAC: Only identities with rollout.edit or rollout.execute may trigger manual rollbacks. Console actions should surface required permissions.

Edge cases and tradeoffs discussed:
- Blue/Green vs Canary: blue/green simplifies rollback but doubles resource footprint; we recommend canary-linear by default for cost reasons, allow blue/green opt-in for high-risk enterprise customers.
- Partial failures during inverse steps: if an inverse op fails, controller should attempt limited retries, then pause and alert SRE; automated compensations should be conservative.
- Cross-tenant dependencies: some rollouts (shared model backends) may need coordinated rollouts. We will mark these as "global-cohort" and require manual operator coordination.

Unresolved questions / follow-ups:
- Do we need a lightweight transactional engine (two-phase commit) across model routing and cache priming? Action: Marco to prototype a coordinator that composes route-splits + cache operations and exposes a dry-run API. (Due: 2024-11-29)
- How to handle rollouts across mixed Dedicated/Private fleets where manifest is submitted to central control plane but execution happens in multiple control domains? Action: Priya + Devon to propose a control-plane handshake pattern and a minimal execution policy for Private deployments. (Due: 2024-12-06)
- Audit retention defaults for changelog/checkpoints (how long to retain signed records). Action: Eleanor to check compliance guidelines and propose retention windows for Standard/Enterprise tiers. (Due: 2024-11-22)

Action items (owners + due dates):
- Marco: Prototype coordinator dry-run API + simple transaction composer. GH: prototype branch -> platform/pilot. Due 2024-11-29.
- Priya + Devon: Draft handshake pattern doc for Private execution + sequence diagrams. Add to Confluence and link from RFC. Due 2024-12-06.
- Eleanor: Retention policy recommendation for changelogs/checkpoints, include storage cost estimate. Due 2024-11-22.
- Aisha: Update RFC with final manifest schema (include required fields from today's decisions) and add example manifests for linear and blue-green strategies. Due 2024-11-20.
- Sam (SRE): Draft runbook for failure modes (partial inverse failure, stuck in PREPARE, network partition) and two-person global kill-switch process. Due 2024-11-27.

Notes-to-self / scribbles (informal):
- Need to standardize event naming: rollout.{id}.step.{n}.validation.{metric|synthetic}.{pass|fail}
- Consider a lightweight sandbox environment where rollouts can be exercised against a "shadow tenant" to catch regressions without consuming customer resources.
- Keep the manifest deliberately compact; heavy-weight orchestration should stay in controller implementation, not in user schema.

Relevant links referenced in meeting:
- RFC draft: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Declarative+Rollouts+RFC
- JIRA: INF-1427 (manifest schema), INF-1473 (rollback automation)
- Prototype PR (starter): https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/982

Next meeting: 2024-11-29 10:00am PST - Marco will demo coordinator prototype and we will review any changes to manifest schema from Aisha's RFC update.

Status: notes captured, RFC to be updated, prototypes + runbooks in flight.
